key_insight: This study audits which mental health interventions 41 language models recommend when identical clinical information comes from a clinician, caregiver, or patient. The supplied abstract describes the audit but does not report whether recommendations differed across these roles.
problem_solved: Mental health advice from language models needs systematic scrutiny, including whether the user's role changes which interventions are recommended despite unchanged clinical facts.
method: Presented 19 clinical case vignettes and five questions from three perspectives: clinician, caregiver, and patient.
Collected 35,055 free-text responses from 41 language models and extracted every named intervention using a validated judge.
Had 29 models rate the full list of intervention options.
impact: The audit provides a framework for testing role-sensitive behavior in mental health AI. Practitioners can use this approach to assess recommendation consistency before deploying models in clinical or patient-facing settings.
visual_elements: Three user icons—clinician, caregiver, and patient—linked to the same clinical vignette.
Audit pipeline: case prompts → model responses → intervention extraction → option ratings.
Scale indicators highlighting 41 models, 19 vignettes, and 35,055 responses.
Comparison-grid template for intervention recommendations across the three user roles, populated only when results are available.
paper_title: Curbside Chatbots: Auditing the Mental Health Interventions Large Language Models Recommend to Clinicians, Caregivers, and Patients
paper_authors: Matthew Flathers, Jill Noorily, Phuong Anh Nguyen, Mark Kalinich, Mina Fallah
